text: Kuh (2008 AAC&U) — identifies 10 high-impact educational practices including capstone courses/projects. Recommends every undergraduate participate in ≥2 high-impact activities across their program.

Wiggins argues school-based assessment should be designed primarily to improve, not audit, student performance: authentic tasks replicate the standards and contexts of adult work, while contrived tasks exist only for efficient grading.

Reviews how teacher-education programs use authentic assessments (cases, exhibitions, portfolios, action research) to support teacher learning, arguing context-embedded performance evidence is more valid for judging teaching than decontextualized tests.

Treats authenticity and directness of performance assessment as promissory validity claims that offset the two major threats to construct validity (construct underrepresentation and construct-irrelevant variance), arguing authentic assessment is fundamentally a quest for complete construct representation.

Empirical study across restructured elementary, middle, and high schools showing authentic pedagogy is strongly associated with authentic academic performance and that the achievement effects are reasonably equitable across student social backgrounds.

Chicago classroom study showing assignments demanding more authentic intellectual work actually improve student scores on conventional standardized tests, refuting the assumption that authentic and standardized assessment are in conflict.

Proposes a five-dimensional framework (task, physical context, social context, assessment result/form, criteria) that operationalizes authenticity for assessment design, grounded in qualitative validation with vocational-nursing students and teachers.

Introduces systemic validity — tests are systemically valid when they induce curricular and instructional changes that foster the cognitive traits the test claims to measure; argues direct (not indirect) assessment is essential.

Argues U.S. education suffers a crisis of over-reliance on summative standardized tests of learning while neglecting classroom assessment for learning, which alone delivers timely feedback that improves student achievement.

Review of 75 studies finds rubric scoring of performance assessments is most reliable when rubrics are analytic, topic-specific, and complemented with exemplars and/or rater training; rubrics do not automatically yield validity but can support it under a richer validity framework.

Identifies two essential rubric components — criteria that target learning (not tasks) and clear descriptions of performance across a quality continuum — and argues analytic rubrics are better suited to formative use because students can see which dimensions need work.

Reviews empirical higher-education rubric research, finding generally positive student perceptions, instructor resistance in some contexts, validity hinging on language clarity, and rubrics enabling reasonably common interpretation of performance across raters.
Introduces kappa as a chance-corrected agreement coefficient for nominal scales, critiquing raw percent agreement for failing to account for the probability that raters coincide by guessing.

Clarifies misconceptions about reliability coefficients in coding tasks and recommends alpha as a generalized chance-corrected agreement statistic that handles any number of raters, any measurement level (nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), and missing data.

Argues interrater reliability is not one concept but three families — consensus (percent agreement, kappa), consistency (correlations), and measurement (G-theory) estimates — each with different assumptions, interpretations, and appropriate uses.

Analyzes 21 studies on formative rubric use and identifies several mediating mechanisms — transparency of expectations, supported self-assessment, feedback scaffolding — through which rubrics improve student performance and self-regulation.

Demonstrates that correlation-based and percent-agreement reliability indices can diverge sharply, and that many portfolio-assessment studies report reliability statistics inappropriate to the scoring design they used.

Dym, Agogino, Eris, Frey & Leifer survey engineering-design pedagogy and argue project-based capstone design is the canonical venue for synthesizing prior coursework, while detailing why design thinking is hard to learn and harder to teach.

Reports the 2005 national survey of 444 engineering capstone programs at 232 institutions covering project logistics, faculty involvement, funding, industry sponsorship, and measures of success; compares to the Todd/Magleby 1994 baseline to surface decadal trends.

Qualitative analysis of interviews with 42 capstone faculty (stratified sample from a national survey) produces a functional taxonomy of pedagogical practices, providing a framework for subsequent studies of teaching-practice/learning-outcome relationships.

Systematic review of 127 SE capstone-course articles (2007-2022) synthesizes a taxonomy across duration, team size, client/project sources, project implementation, and student assessment; finds the modal course is one semester with 4-5 person teams building proof-of-concept software for an external client.

Describes a multi-year SE capstone redesigned as a simulated software-development company spanning multiple student cohorts, with intended learning outcomes, teaching/learning activities, and assessment tasks aligned to organizational, process, and communication competencies rather than only technical deliverables.

Working-group study collecting instructor perspectives across computing-field capstone courses; documents how faculty conceive of capstone goals, assessment criteria, and team-dynamics challenges, complementing the SE-only systematic review with broader computing coverage.

Case study of a cross-disciplinary (computer/electrical/mechanical) FSAE electric-vehicle capstone, with explicit mapping of project artifacts to each of the seven ABET student outcomes and the assessment instruments used.

Jointly issued by AERA/APA/NCME, the Standards define operational best practice for validity, fairness, reliability, design, delivery, scoring, and use of tests; the canonical reference for the validity argument underlying credentialing-exam claims.

C-BEN consortium framework defining quality elements for CBE programs spanning learner experience, learning outcomes, instructional/learning processes, assessment, and credentialing; explicit articulation of faculty roles in validating mastery via assessment portfolios.

Defines computing-discipline competency as the integration of contextualized knowledge, skills, and dispositions, drawing on IT2017, SWECOM, and SFIA; established the framework that fed the ACM/IEEE Computing Curricula 2020 (CC2020) competency model.

Synthesizes validity evidence for programmatic assessment — using many low-stakes assessments aggregated into high-stakes competency decisions — and argues that competency judgments require a triangulated body of evidence rather than any single test.

Specialty-tier credential validating expertise in building and deploying ML solutions on AWS; recommends 2+ years of hands-on ML/DL workloads on AWS; multiple-choice exam with scaled score 100-1000 and passing cutoff 750. Scheduled retirement March 2026 (superseded by the MLA-C01 Associate-tier ML Engineer cert).

Successor cert that replaces the retiring ML Specialty; exam guide enumerates task statements across data preparation, model development, deployment/orchestration, and ML solutions monitoring — concretizing the operational ML competency domain a vendor regards as bookable.

Defines six task domains (architect low-code AI solutions; collaborate to manage data and models; scale prototypes to ML models; serve and scale models; automate/orchestrate ML pipelines; monitor AI solutions) with domain weightings; 50-60 questions, 2 hours, $200.

Vendor-neutral data-analyst credential structured across five domains (Data Concepts & Environments; Data Acquisition & Preparation; Data Analysis; Visualization & Reporting; Data Governance); ~90 questions, passing score 675 on a scaled scale.

Reports five iterations of research from the Inter/National Coalition for Electronic Portfolio Research across 20 institutions, examining effects on reflection, integrative learning, identity, organizational learning, and technology-supported learning design.

Synthesizes data from the Connect to Learning network across 24 campuses and proposes the Catalyst Framework (Inquiry, Reflection, Integration; Pedagogy, Professional Development, Outcomes Assessment, Technology, Scaling Up) as the design backbone for high-impact ePortfolio implementations.

Twenty case studies from institutions ranging from Bronx Community College to Yale, Arizona State, and Dublin City University, illustrating how the Catalyst Framework plays out across two-year colleges, R1s, and discipline-specific programs.

Lays out a six-task iterative framework for designing course- and program-level ePortfolio implementations, with explicit guidance on showcase vs developmental vs assessment portfolio choices and on integrating ePortfolios into institutional assessment efforts.

Edited reference with contributions from 50+ ePortfolio practitioners; provides an authoritative account of ePortfolio dimensions (pedagogy, reflection, integrative learning, technology, assessment) along with international case studies.

Systematic review of ePortfolio research since 1996 finding that the majority is theory-based argumentation or descriptive practitioner accounts; a minority present original empirical data on user perceptions or student outcomes, with even fewer measuring against learning theory.

Documents AAC&U 16 cross-cutting VALUE rubrics, their faculty-driven development process, validity/reliability evidence from the multi-state VALUE pilot, and explicit pairing with ePortfolio collections for direct assessment across curriculum, co-curriculum, and beyond.

Sixteen open-license rubrics covering essential learning outcomes (Critical Thinking, Written Communication, Integrative Learning, etc.); the Integrative Learning rubric was explicitly designed for ePortfolio-style work collections.

Distinguishes reflection-in-action (real-time reframing while working) from reflection-on-action (retrospective analysis), arguing that professional schools over-rely on technical rationality and underweight the tacit-knowledge work practitioners actually do.

Operationalises the reflective-practitioner concept into curriculum design via the practicum — coached studio-style learning in which students confront ill-structured problems, get expert feedback, and develop reflection-in-action habits.

Articulates the Boud-Keogh-Walker three-stage reflection model (returning to experience, attending to feelings, re-evaluating experience), explicitly framing reflection as the mechanism that converts raw experience into actionable learning.

Reframes self-assessment as a tool for developing students informed evaluative judgment for future learning, rather than as a self-grading exercise; argues sustainable assessment must build judgment that outlasts the course.

Maps reflective-writing techniques (learning journals, double-entry logs, reflective essays) onto Dewey/Schon/Boud theoretical lineages, with concrete prompt families and quality criteria for academic reflection.

Defines criteria-referenced self-assessment as a three-step formative process (collect performance evidence, compare to stated criteria, revise) and argues it must remain non-graded to preserve its learning function.

Reviews 76 empirical studies (2013-2018) on student self-assessment, finding consistent positive associations with achievement and self-regulated learning but documenting accuracy limitations (especially for novice and low-achieving students) and student-perception caveats.

Articulates the three-phase cyclical model of self-regulated learning (forethought, performance, self-reflection) and positions metacognitive self-monitoring as the engine that links reflection to subsequent strategy choice.
